questions.text:
An array [latex]A [/latex] of length [latex]n [/latex] with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index [latex]1 \leq i \leq n [/latex] such that [latex]A[1..i] [/latex] is sorted in the non-decreasing order and [latex]A[i+1..n] [/latex] is sorted in the non-increasing order.
Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array [latex]A [/latex]?
questions.solution:
A bitonic array first increases then decreases (or vice versa). At any index, comparing the current element to its neighbors tells you which "half" (increasing or decreasing) you're in, and binary search can be adapted to search each half:

First locate the peak (maximum) element using a binary-search-style approach in [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex] (comparing an element to its neighbors to decide which direction has the larger values). Once the peak is found, the array splits into two ordinary sorted sequences (one increasing, one decreasing), and each can be searched with ordinary binary search, also [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex].

Combining these steps keeps the total worst-case comparisons at [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex], matching what you'd get for a single sorted array — no better bound like [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex] is achievable (you must still narrow down the location), and no worse bound like [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] or [latex]\Theta(\log^2n)[/latex] is necessary.

Answer: Θ(log n)

questions.text: Let [latex] A [/latex] be an array containing integer values. The distance of [latex] A [/latex] is defined as the minimum number of elements in [latex] A [/latex] that must be replaced with another integer so that the resulting array is sorted in non-decreasing order. The distance of the array [latex] [2,5,3,1,4,2,6] [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
Elements we keep must already be in non-decreasing order; all others can be replaced by suitable values. So
distance = [latex]n-[/latex] (length of longest non-decreasing subsequence).

In [2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 6] the longest non-decreasing subsequence is 2, 3, 4, 6 (length 4).

Distance [latex]=7-4=3[/latex] (e.g. [2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 6]).

Answer: 3

questions.text: What is the worst-case number of arithmetic operations performed by recursive binary search on a sorted array of size n?
questions.solution:
Each recursive call does a constant number of arithmetic operations (computing mid) and halves the range. The depth is [latex]\log_2 n[/latex], so the total is [latex]\Theta(\log_2 n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(\log_2(n))[/latex]

questions.text: Let P be an array containing n integers. Let t be the lowest upper bound on the number of comparisons of the array elements, required to find the minimum and maximum values in an arbitrary array of n elements. Which one of the following choices is correct?
questions.solution:
Process elements in pairs: compare the two, then compare the smaller with the current min and the larger with the current max. That is 3 comparisons per 2 elements: about [latex]\lceil3n/2\rceil-2[/latex] comparisons, and this is optimal.

So [latex]t \gt n[/latex] and [latex]t\le3\lceil n/2\rceil[/latex].

Answer: [latex]t \gt n[/latex] and [latex]t\le3\lceil\frac n2\rceil[/latex]

questions.text: If an array A contains the items 10, 4, 7, 23, 67, 12 and 5 in that order, what will be the resultant array A after third pass of insertion sort?
questions.solution:
Insertion sort, inserting one element per pass:
- Pass 1 (insert 4): 4, 10, 7, 23, 67, 12, 5
- Pass 2 (insert 7): 4, 7, 10, 23, 67, 12, 5
- Pass 3 (insert 23): already in place [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4, 7, 10, 23, 67, 12, 5

Answer: 4, 7, 10, 23, 67, 12, 5
